clue.text: Artist puts money in older frame

indicators.note: the money is placed in the older frame, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: SR is the abbreviation for senior, that is older
pence are British coins, so money

explanation.surface: A painter sinks cash into an antique picture frame.
explanation.walkthrough: 'frame' backs up the containment signal. Stanley Spencer was an English painter of Cookham scenes.
explanation.definitionFit: Stanley Spencer was a twentieth-century English painter, so an example of the category.

clue.text: Well supported south-eastern writer

indicators.note: in a down entry a supported word stands below the piece holding it up, so the second piece comes after

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A popular author from the south-east of England.
explanation.walkthrough: Anna Sewell wrote Black Beauty.
explanation.definitionFit: Anna Sewell was the English novelist who wrote Black Beauty, an example of an author.

clue.text: Climbing volume I have is quite exciting

indicators.note: in a down entry climbing means the word for volume is read upwards, so backwards

parts.note: a tome is a large book, a volume
I've is the contraction of these two words

explanation.surface: A book rising up the bestseller list is thrilling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Climbing' turns TOME upwards to give EMOT.
explanation.definitionFit: Something emotive stirs strong feeling, which is a fair stretch of rousing or exciting.

clue.text: Violent seizure due to pact being torn up

indicators.note: a treaty torn up is destroyed, so these letters are broken apart and rearranged

explanation.surface: A treaty is ripped up, and a forcible takeover follows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'being torn up' rearranges DUE TO PACT into the French phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: A coup d'etat is a sudden forcible seizure of state power.

clue.text: Europe has not yet recovered from it, thought Oliver St John Gogarty

definitions.text: Europe has not yet recovered from it, thought Oliver St John Gogarty

parts.words: Europe has not yet recovered from it, thought Oliver St John Gogarty
parts.note: the Irish wit Gogarty quipped that Europe was still reeling from the great rebirth of art and learning in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries

explanation.surface: An Irish writer's verdict on some historic upheaval Europe never got over.
explanation.definitionFit: The rebirth of classical learning from the fourteenth century is the historic period Gogarty's quip refers to.

clue.text: A tenacious sounding emperor's son-in-law

indicators.note: the word for tenacious is said aloud rather than spelt, so its sound gives the letters

parts.note: a tenacious thing is a gripper, holding on tight

explanation.surface: An emperor's relative by marriage is remembered for holding on tightly.
explanation.walkthrough: In a non-rhotic accent GRIPPER sounds like the end of the name. Marcus Agrippa married Julia, daughter of the emperor Augustus.
explanation.definitionFit: Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa married Julia, daughter of Augustus, becoming the first Roman emperor's son-in-law.

clue.text: Academician comes back to model! in painting

indicators.note: the academician returns, so the letters for him are read backwards

parts.note: RA stands for Royal Academician
the Model T was Henry Ford's famous car

explanation.surface: A Royal Academy member returns to his sitter, absorbed in his canvas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'comes back' turns RA into AR; the Model T Ford supplies T.
explanation.definitionFit: Painting is one of the fine arts, so the general term covers it.

clue.text: Amiable Cotswold drinking companion?

parts.note: Laurie Lee's Cotswold memoir pairs the drink cider with a girl's name, the friendly companion of its title

explanation.surface: A friendly partner for a pint in a Gloucestershire village pub.
explanation.walkthrough: Laurie Lee's Cider with Rosie is set in Slad in the Cotswolds; the girl in the title is the one you drink cider with.
explanation.definitionFit: In Lee's memoir title she is the girl who shares the cider, hence a drinking companion.

clue.text: William Irish's lady recalling Vernon Lee's lover

explanation.surface: Two writers' romantic partners compared.
explanation.definitionFit: William Irish wrote the thriller Phantom Lady, and Vernon Lee the ghost story A Phantom Lover, so the word fits both titles.

clue.text: "Perhaps she wished an-profounder,/ But whatsoever she wished, she acted right" (Byron)

definitions.text: "Perhaps she wished an-profounder,/ But whatsoever she wished, she acted right" (Byron)

parts.words: "Perhaps she wished an-profounder,/ But whatsoever she wished, she acted right" (Byron)
parts.note: the missing word in Byron's Don Juan couplet is a hopeful suitor who wished to be deeper

explanation.surface: A Byron couplet about a woman who wanted a deeper admirer but behaved well.
explanation.walkthrough: Fill the gap in the quotation from Don Juan.
explanation.definitionFit: The gap in Byron's couplet is filled by a word for an ambitious candidate or hopeful suitor.

clue.text: The answer is a question, to which 12 may have a clue

definitions.text: The answer is a question, to which 12 may have a clue

parts.words: The answer is a question, to which 12 may have a clue
parts.note: the word is a garbled query asking who committed the crime, and the detective of 12 across holds clues to it

explanation.surface: A riddle whose answer is itself a question that a detective might solve.
explanation.walkthrough: The name for a crime novel is ungrammatical 'Who done it?'; 12 across is INSPECTOR, who collects clues.
explanation.definitionFit: A detective story is named for its question about the culprit, which an investigator answers from clues.

clue.text: Second instrument used by Thackeray character

parts.note: a harp is a stringed musical instrument

explanation.surface: A Victorian novelist's creation plays a backup instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: Becky Sharp is the scheming heroine of Thackeray's Vanity Fair.
explanation.definitionFit: Becky Sharp is the adventuress at the centre of Vanity Fair, an example of a Thackeray creation.

clue.text: Sandy McAllister, for example (oddly enough, there's some Irish in the boy)

indicators.note: the Irish piece sits in the boy, one inside the other

parts.note: a lad is a boy

explanation.surface: A Scotsman's name prompts a joke about an Irish streak in a lad.
explanation.walkthrough: Sandy McAllister is the Scottish painter nicknamed the Laird in du Maurier's Trilby.
explanation.definitionFit: In Trilby the Scottish artist Sandy McAllister is called by the Scots title for a landowner.

clue.text: Examine alternative for Priestley's caller

parts.note: to inspect is to examine closely
or is the word that introduces an alternative

explanation.surface: A suggestion to scrutinise another candidate for the visitor in a play.
explanation.walkthrough: J.B. Priestley's play is An Inspector Calls.
explanation.definitionFit: In Priestley's An Inspector Calls the visiting police officer is the one who calls.

clue.text: One of Hulme's conjectures?

parts.note: T.E. Hulme's essays were collected under a title meaning guesses or theories, so one of them is a single such guess

explanation.surface: A question about one theory put forward by the philosopher T.E. Hulme.
explanation.definitionFit: A conjecture is a guess or theory, and Hulme's posthumous collection bore the plural of this word.

clue.text: Strangely rude first names of Miss Garlands unwanted suitor

indicators.note: strangely means the letters are put into an odd new order

explanation.surface: A heroine's suitor bears oddly coarse given names.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strangely' rearranges RUDE FIRST NAMES. In Hardy's The Trumpet-Major the boastful yeoman Festus Derriman pursues Anne Garland.
explanation.definitionFit: Festus Derriman is the cowardly yeoman who courts Anne Garland in vain in Hardy's The Trumpet-Major.

clue.text: Brutally rid Wagner of what's gratifying

indicators.note: treated brutally, the letters are knocked about into a new order

explanation.surface: A harsh demand to be rid of Wagner's music, which some would find pleasing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brutally' rearranges RID WAGNER.
explanation.definitionFit: Something rewarding brings satisfaction, so it is gratifying.

clue.text: "I have a dream", Rolf Boldrewood may have had him say

definitions.text: "I have a dream", Rolf Boldrewood may have had him say

parts.words: "I have a dream", Rolf Boldrewood may have had him say
parts.note: Boldrewood wrote a novel titled after the dream of an Australian settler on unclaimed land, who might well say these words

explanation.surface: An Australian novelist imagined putting a famous civil-rights line into a character's mouth.
explanation.walkthrough: Rolf Boldrewood's novel is The Squatter's Dream; in Australia a squatter held large tracts of pastoral land.
explanation.definitionFit: Boldrewood's novel The Squatter's Dream gives its settler hero the dream the quotation claims.

clue.text: The Varlet with the Velvet Pouch

definitions.text: The Varlet with the Velvet Pouch

parts.words: The Varlet with the Velvet Pouch
parts.note: a chapter in a Walter Scott novel of Louis XI's France, naming its Scottish archer hero

explanation.surface: A fairy-tale title about a servant carrying a soft purse.
explanation.walkthrough: Scott's Quentin Durward follows a young Scot in the guard of Louis XI.
explanation.definitionFit: Scott's novel about a Scottish archer at Louis XI's court contains this episode.

clue.text: Play involving one's mate, perhaps

explanation.surface: A drama about a friend, possibly.
explanation.walkthrough: Beckett's play is the first sense; in chess the final phase may end with checkmate.
explanation.definitionFit: Beckett wrote the play of this name, and in chess the closing phase may involve checkmate.

clue.text: Harmonist keeps a very quiet interior in ceremony

indicators.note: the ceremony keeps the other letters, holding them inside

parts.note: a rite is a ceremony
pp is the musical marking pianissimo, very quiet

explanation.surface: A musical type stays hushed throughout a ritual.
explanation.walkthrough: The Harmony Society were followers of George Rapp in nineteenth-century America.
explanation.definitionFit: Harmonists were members of George Rapp's religious community, so they were called after its founder.

clue.text: Hollow identification of Herbert

explanation.surface: An empty space where a man's name should be.
explanation.walkthrough: Herbert Pocket is Pip's friend in Dickens's Great Expectations.
explanation.definitionFit: A hollow is a cavity or pouch, and Herbert in Great Expectations bears this surname.

clue.text: Daughter of Cassiopeia carried by Arabian dromedary

indicators.note: the letters are carried by these words, sitting inside them

explanation.surface: A princess rides on a camel through the desert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'carried by' hides the name in ArabiAN DROMEDAry.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the princess chained to a rock was the child of Cepheus and Cassiopeia.

clue.text: Feline quantity of civet requested of Gloucester by Lear

definitions.text: quantity of civet requested of Gloucester by Lear

explanation.surface: A cat and a measure of perfume asked for in a Shakespeare play.
explanation.walkthrough: In King Lear, Lear says 'Give me an ounce of civet, good apothecary' in his scene with blinded Gloucester.
explanation.definitionFit: The snow leopard is also called by this name, and Lear asks for this weight of perfume.

clue.text: Concerning professional modern copy

parts.note: re means about or concerning
pro is short for professional

explanation.surface: A matter concerning a professional's up-to-date reproduction.
explanation.definitionFit: A repro is a reproduction, a recent imitation of an original piece.

clue.text: An American humorist or two

explanation.surface: A US comic writer, or perhaps a pair of them.
explanation.walkthrough: Mark Twain is the humorist; twain is old English for two.
explanation.definitionFit: Mark Twain was the US humorist, and the archaic word for a pair is the same.

clue.text: 'I'm skeered to the marrow,… because I'm out of my -' (R. D. Saunders)

definitions.text: 'I'm skeered to the marrow,… because I'm out of my -' (R. D. Saunders)

parts.words: 'I'm skeered to the marrow,… because I'm out of my -' (R. D. Saunders)
parts.note: the speaker is frightened because he is away from his own district, his home patch, which fills the gap

explanation.surface: A frightened speaker in a quoted line admits being out of his element.
explanation.walkthrough: Fill the gap in the quotation: someone out of their own district or area of expertise.
explanation.definitionFit: The gap needs a word for one's own district or sphere of competence.

clue.text: Wader decapitated, twice

indicators.note: the head of the bird is cut off, losing its first letter

parts.note: the ibis is a long-legged wading bird

explanation.surface: A wading bird loses its head two times over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'decapitated' removes the I that begins IBIS.
explanation.definitionFit: Bis is the Latin-derived musical direction meaning repeat, that is, do it two times.

clue.text: Whose mind did Edgar Wallace explore?

definitions.text: Whose mind did Edgar Wallace explore?

parts.words: Whose mind did Edgar Wallace explore?
parts.note: Wallace wrote The Mind of Mr J.G. Reeder about a quiet detective, so the question asks for the detective's surname in possessive form

explanation.surface: A question about which character's thoughts a thriller writer investigated.
explanation.walkthrough: Edgar Wallace's book is The Mind of Mr J.G. Reeder; the possessive matches 'Whose'.
explanation.definitionFit: Wallace's collection The Mind of Mr J.G. Reeder explores that detective's thinking.

clue.text: It was Cowper's potent quack's "most tender mercy"

definitions.text: It was Cowper's potent quack's "most tender mercy"

parts.words: It was Cowper's potent quack's "most tender mercy"
parts.note: in Cowper's poem the powerful quack doctor shows his kindest mercy by leaving the patient alone, a failure to attend

explanation.surface: A quotation from Cowper about a charlatan doctor's gentlest kindness.
explanation.walkthrough: In Cowper's verse the quack's 'most tender mercy is neglect': leaving you alone is the kindest thing he does.
explanation.definitionFit: Failing to attend to something is the sense, the quack's kindest mercy being to leave the patient alone.
